Mermaid source

Preferred syntax: block. Fixed categorical cells; membership appears in comments.

Framing

How a corpus reads where it stands and what comes next, drawn from the graph. First the architecture the views stand on: a review of which engine units are significant enough to anchor, and the meaning of each role they carry. Then the capability map, epics with their features and stories, and the Protocol's own capabilities stated as epics. Then the diagrams the graph has data for, and the design slice, a Pack read as one design with the architecture it touches. Last the roadmap: the decision that lets the graph hold an advisory priority, the roadmap reading and its page and memo, and the decision that lets the roadmap replace the Protocol's numbered plans.

specs/protocol/significant-units-review.sdp.md

No open questions and no blocking questions; implementation binding present, verifier binding present, and expected-outcome oracle none.

A designer needs to find the contracts, decisions and stages a change must preserve. The accepted set records those units on the code that owns them. Exporting a helper, appearing in an import ranking or giving a file an impact answer does not by itself earn an identity.

Intent
outcome
Keep the accepted set focused on the engine's significant contracts, decisions and stages, with meaningful roles and architectural uses, and exclude units anchored only for coverage.

Design view

Requirement drawing

  • Declared verifying examples: no declared verifying example.

Decisions

  • spec:decisions.anchor-binding-grain

    On a code anchor, satisfies is optional and plural; on a test anchor, verifies is plural and non-empty. The constant form accepts one ref(…) or a fresh array literal of them. Each resolving target confers its fact, and implemented stays a whole-Spec fact. An anchored edge references runs from a CodeNode to a Spec, from references?: readonly SpecId[] on a code anchor; it may target any Spec, decisions included, confers no delivery fact, moves no readiness floor, and the drift alarm ignores it. It says this code answers to that design without claiming to realize it: the unit follows the design without realizing any of its promises, or realizes part of a Spec whose remaining promises no unit yet realizes, so a change to the design asks the code to follow. A design that builds on existing code states that by a typed relation to the Spec the code satisfies, never by a reference from the code. A target named in both satisfies and references is an error. An identity-only code anchor, with no satisfies and no references, is lawful: it mints a CodeNode for structure and for byFile, and nothing else.

  • spec:decisions.architectural-annotation

    Architectural significance is annotated on the anchor of the unit that realizes it. A code anchor may carry role, the architectural pattern the unit plays; a component: anchor may additionally carry layer, one of edge, application, domain, adapter, or infrastructure, and context, its bounded context. The component: anchor is anchored architecture: it is the declared component, and there is no separate architecture file, because the anchor sits where the component is realized. It is not the original design's declared Component that could exist before code; an unrealized component lives in Specs and never as an invented CodeNode. A role is a free, corpus-owned vocabulary whose taxonomy the census renders with counts from the graph; service, decider, projection, read-model, codec, contract, barrel, and utility are the lineage set, not a closed list. layer is a closed set, and a value outside it is an envelope error; layer or context on a non-component anchor is an envelope error. All three attributes are optional, and omission is lawful.

specs/protocol/role-vocabulary.sdp.md

No open questions and no blocking questions; implementation binding present, verifier binding none, and expected-outcome oracle none.

Authors choose a role by the architectural responsibility a unit owns. The same responsibility uses the same word across the engine. These definitions are this corpus's design vocabulary, not a Protocol enum or a registry a validator checks. An adopter may use other roles for its own architecture.

Intent
outcome
Define each architectural role the engine's anchors use, so the accepted set of significant units reads as a curated register of the engine's patterns and abstractions.
Model
adapter · term.adapter line 22 · specs/protocol/role-vocabulary.sdp.md:22
Connects an external tool or runtime to an engine contract, such as a test runner or a TypeScript import reader.
codec · term.codec line 23 · specs/protocol/role-vocabulary.sdp.md:23
Parses, normalizes or encodes a representation while preserving the meaning owned by its contract, such as ids, carrier text, parameter input or source links.
contract · term.contract line 24 · specs/protocol/role-vocabulary.sdp.md:24
Owns a shared interface, data shape, closed vocabulary or public boundary that independently developed callers and providers must agree on.
decider · term.decider line 25 · specs/protocol/role-vocabulary.sdp.md:25
Computes a semantic answer from explicit inputs without reading or writing external state, such as delivery facts or example eligibility.
extractor · term.extractor line 26 · specs/protocol/role-vocabulary.sdp.md:26
Reads authored carriers or source bindings, or composes their reified results, into the graph and its located evidence.
interaction · term.interaction line 27 · specs/protocol/role-vocabulary.sdp.md:27
Adds browser controls and feedback to build-rendered content without owning its graph joins or layout. This is a corpus role for optional element behavior.
projection · term.projection line 28 · specs/protocol/role-vocabulary.sdp.md:28
Derives read-only presentation or generated contract content from the graph, the reader or an explicitly supplied answer. A page fragment and a complete page use the same role when both own presentation.

Decisions

  • spec:decisions.architectural-annotation

    Architectural significance is annotated on the anchor of the unit that realizes it. A code anchor may carry role, the architectural pattern the unit plays; a component: anchor may additionally carry layer, one of edge, application, domain, adapter, or infrastructure, and context, its bounded context. The component: anchor is anchored architecture: it is the declared component, and there is no separate architecture file, because the anchor sits where the component is realized. It is not the original design's declared Component that could exist before code; an unrealized component lives in Specs and never as an invented CodeNode. A role is a free, corpus-owned vocabulary whose taxonomy the census renders with counts from the graph; service, decider, projection, read-model, codec, contract, barrel, and utility are the lineage set, not a closed list. layer is a closed set, and a value outside it is an envelope error; layer or context on a non-component anchor is an envelope error. All three attributes are optional, and omission is lawful.

specs/consumers/capability-map.sdp.md

No open questions and no blocking questions; implementation binding present, verifier binding present, and expected-outcome oracle none.

The map answers what a corpus intends to do before a reader chooses a Pack. Refinement can skip an altitude, repeat an altitude, or give a Spec several parents. The map keeps that structure. An epic's descendants are a set of Specs, not a measure of completion.

Intent
actor
A person or agent choosing which capability's design to read.
problem
An altitude filter gives a flat list and Pack membership does not explain refinement.
outcome
Read every epic with its refinement descendants, its design maturity and direct binding evidence, and expose every Spec no epic reaches.
Behavior
rule.graphOnly line 29 · specs/consumers/capability-map.sdp.md:29
The map follows only declared refines edges between resolving Specs, from parent to child for reading. It reads every kind at every altitude, preserves intermediate Specs, and derives no parent from a title, path, Pack, dependency or binding.

Every Spec at epic altitude is an entry, whatever its kind. An epic may itself refine another epic; both remain selectable, and a parent's descendant set includes the nested epic and its descendants.

An epic's rollup counts distinct descendants, excluding the epic itself, by stated rung, floor reached, kind and altitude; it counts those with implementation bindings and those with verifier bindings separately. Open and blocking question totals count the questions on those distinct descendants. Rollups for overlapping epics are never added to form a corpus total.

Examples and decisions participate in reach, counts and edges like every other kind. The page may fold them into labelled disclosures, but exposes their rows and any descendants they parent. rule.unreached line 35 · specs/consumers/capability-map.sdp.md:35
A Spec is unreached when no epic reaches it, counting an epic as reaching itself. The answer lists every unreached id, including examples and decisions, and groups the unreached subgraph by its roots. A branch that is also reached remains outside that subgraph, with its cross-edge retained in the full answer.

Unresolved or non-Spec refinement endpoints are reported in damage and excluded from traversal. Cyclic refinement is reported as sorted groups whose members all reach one another, including self-links. Traversal visits each id once per root. The map displays the damage without inventing ancestry or withholding the rest.

criteria
  • A diamond retains both parent edges, lists the shared child once in nodes, and counts it once in that epic's descendants.
  • A corpus with no epics still exposes every Spec; a cyclic unreached component has a root and finite traversal.
  • An epic with a bound example and a ratified decision counts both descendants while retaining its own empty delivery facts.
  • Summary and full answers have identical totals, epic rollups, cycles and damage; the summary names every omitted field.
  • An epic selection includes its whole reachable set and no unrelated roots; invalid parameters return diagnostics without a plausible empty map.

5. Capability epics keep kind independent of altitude

spec:decisions.epics-of-any-kind

Capability epics keep kind independent of altitude

spec:decisions.epics-of-any-kindDecision Record · featureready floor ready

Packs: pack:roadmaps-and-slices-v1, pack:self-hosting-v1

Design: no design entries · no pinned declarations · no decisions

Findings: no errors, no warnings

specs/decisions/epics-of-any-kind.sdp.md

No open questions and no blocking questions; implementation binding none, verifier binding none, and expected-outcome oracle none.

Intent
outcome
Decide whether a capability map admits epics of every kind or only behavior epics.
Decision
context
The glossary row for capability and domain names a Capability Map over high-altitude behavior Specs, while kind and altitude are independent descriptors on the one primitive, and the hubs that already state the Protocol's capabilities include a domain model, a projection model and the rule that separates the two check families.
decision
Any Spec stated at epic altitude is an epic, whatever its kind, and keeps its kind: the capability map reads every epic and its refinement descendants, and the glossary row broadens from high-altitude behavior Specs to epic Specs of every kind.
rationale
  • Hard to reverse: corpora organize their capabilities around which Specs may be epics, and the capability map, its page and the upgrade guide read that choice. Surprising without context: the ratified glossary row limited the map to behavior Specs, so a reader needs to know why a model or a rule now heads a capability. A real trade-off: an epic of any kind keeps the Spec that already owns a capability's outcome as its head, as the one-primitive decision's named coordinates already imply, against a map whose roots differ in kind and a glossary row that changes.
alternatives
  • Keep behavior-only capability epics and introduce behavior wrappers over the model and rule hubs: each wrapper would restate an outcome another Spec already owns, a second owner that drifts, only so that a view can read it.
consequences
  • The capability map draws epics of every kind, each labelled with its kind, and a Spec's kind never decides whether it heads a capability.
  • The glossary row for capability and domain names a Capability Map over epic Specs of every kind and their refinement descendants.

6. The Protocol organizes its own features in capability epics

spec:protocol.capability-epics

The Protocol organizes its own features in capability epics

spec:protocol.capability-epicsUse Case / Behavior · featureready floor ready

Packs: pack:roadmaps-and-slices-v1, pack:self-hosting-v1

Design: 5 design entries · no pinned declarations · 1 decision

Findings: no errors, no warnings

specs/protocol/capability-epics.sdp.md

No open questions and no blocking questions; implementation binding present, verifier binding present, and expected-outcome oracle none.

An epic states an enduring intended outcome. Where an existing hub owns an outcome, enlarging its altitude preserves its identity, kind, evidence and bindings. Self-hosting describes the Protocol using itself; it is not the parent of every capability offered to an adopter.

Intent
outcome
Organize the Protocol's capabilities through explicit refinement so a reader can choose a capability and inspect its design and bindings.
Behavior
rule.epicHome line 25 · specs/protocol/capability-epics.sdp.md:25
Enrich an existing hub to epic altitude when its intended outcome already names the capability. Keep its id, kind and truth; author a new epic only when no existing Spec owns that outcome. A model or rule can be an epic without becoming behavior merely to appear in the map.

no example exercises it

rule.refinement line 26 · specs/protocol/capability-epics.sdp.md:26
Each feature belongs under the epic whose intended outcome it makes more precise, directly or through intermediate Specs. Existing genuine refinement remains, including a nested epic and multiple parents. A Pack, path or dependency alone does not establish that relationship.

no example exercises it

rule.selfHosting line 27 · specs/protocol/capability-epics.sdp.md:27
The self-hosting epic keeps the Protocol's own use of the carrier, structural binding, roadmap and capability organization, and the decisions about that practice and the Protocol's identity. General model, derivation, validation and projection capabilities no longer refine self-hosting merely because the corpus exercises them.

no example exercises it

rule.preserveEvidence line 28 · specs/protocol/capability-epics.sdp.md:28
A re-altituded hub keeps its readiness statement when its content still supports it; reparenting confers no delivery fact and adds no anchor.

no example exercises it

0 unkeyed rules.

Design
epicHome line 32 · specs/protocol/capability-epics.sdp.md:32
reuse an existing outcome owner so altitude changes do not duplicate intent; add an epic only for an outcome no hub already states. Design iteration has no epic: no Spec owns that outcome, its features are views and reader recipes that refine the projection and agent capabilities, and its Pack already groups them for review.
carrierHome line 33 · specs/protocol/capability-epics.sdp.md:33
the Markdown hub names the default authoring entry, while its rule puts Markdown and TypeScript on one graph path and its carrier ruling admits Gherkin. Its existing descendants refine that shared authoring outcome, so it keeps its identity and title.
executableHome line 34 · specs/protocol/capability-epics.sdp.md:34
the runner owns step dispatch and failure rendering, and contract generation owns typed contracts. Neither owns the whole outcome of executing an example against its authored intent, so a separate executable-examples epic joins those refinements. Their other genuine refinement and dependency relations remain.
nestedEpic line 35 · specs/protocol/capability-epics.sdp.md:35
the agent capability remains a refinement of the projection capability because scripted graph access is a consumer-specific view. Its descendants belong to both epic scopes, and the map reports that overlap explicitly.
corpusChecks line 36 · specs/protocol/capability-epics.sdp.md:36
corpus-selected rules refine the agent capability because their intended operation is scripting the graph; the validation command is their host, while their findings remain outside the Protocol's conformance and honesty families. A refinement states the narrower outcome and a dependency states what must hold: both relations intentionally connect the build pipeline to derivation, corpus rules to the agent capability, and architecture and external-register checks to corpus rules.

specs/extraction/executable-examples.sdp.md

No open questions and no blocking questions; implementation binding present, verifier binding none, and expected-outcome oracle none.

The capability connects authored intent to an example's execution. Contract generation and the runner own narrower parts of that outcome; neither alone owns it. A change to the authored example must reach its test through the generated contract.

Intent
actor
An author binding an example to a test of the intended behavior.
problem
A separately handwritten test can drift from the Spec's own steps and expected outcome.
outcome
Run an example against its authored intent through graph-derived contracts and report failures in the words of its steps.
Behavior
rule.authoredSteps line 23 · specs/extraction/executable-examples.sdp.md:23
Execution reads the steps and bound values from contracts derived from the graph; it adds no second authored description of the example.

no example exercises it

rule.binding line 24 · specs/extraction/executable-examples.sdp.md:24
A bound test supplies the world and step handlers, and the runner executes the contract's steps in authored order. Contract generation and execution keep their separate responsibilities.

no example exercises it

rule.failure line 25 · specs/extraction/executable-examples.sdp.md:25
A failing step names the authored intent it exercised. An unspecified expected outcome remains explicit and cannot become a passing comparison by assumption.

no example exercises it

8. The capability map page makes refinement readable by epic

spec:consumers.spec-studio.capability-map-page

The capability map page makes refinement readable by epic

spec:consumers.spec-studio.capability-map-pageUse Case / Behavior · storyready floor ready

Packs: pack:roadmaps-and-slices-v1, pack:self-hosting-v1

Design: 6 design entries · 1 pinned declaration · no decisions

Findings: no errors, no warnings

specs/consumers/spec-studio.capability-map-page.sdp.md

No open questions and no blocking questions; implementation binding present, verifier binding present, and expected-outcome oracle none.

Intent
actor
A reviewer looking for a capability before choosing a Spec or Pack.
problem
A flat altitude filter hides how a capability is decomposed, and a large refinement drawing becomes unreadable when shrunk to the page width.
outcome
Read an epic overview, inspect its refinement structure and evidence, and narrow the index's Specs to its descendants.
Behavior
rule.page line 32 · specs/consumers/spec-studio.capability-map-page.sdp.md:32
The Studio publishes capabilities.html on every build and links it as Capabilities immediately after Packs in the top navigation. The Packs lens keeps its membership order and the index remains the landing page.

no example exercises it

rule.recipeData line 33 · specs/consumers/spec-studio.capability-map-page.sdp.md:33
The page reads recipe 52 with { detail: true } and no epic parameter. It renders every epic's own evidence beside its descendant rollup and names the rollup's scope. Examples and decisions have separate counts and expandable rows. There is no combined total obtained by adding epic rows.

no example exercises it

rule.drawing line 34 · specs/consumers/spec-studio.capability-map-page.sdp.md:34
Each epic has a refinement drawing supplied by the shared diagram implementation. It keeps parent-to-child reading order while arrows, if drawn, point child to parent and the legend says refines. Repeated nodes link to their first occurrence within that epic section. A nested epic remains a labelled epic, not a new altitude.

no example exercises it

rule.bounded line 35 · specs/consumers/spec-studio.capability-map-page.sdp.md:35
A large branch folds at the shared diagram bound and links to its complete refinement text. At desktop width it never scales labels below the shared legibility size to fit an entire tree; below the responsive breakpoint it follows the shared legibility rule's narrow fit. The text includes every node and edge, repeats and cyclic links labelled in words, and stays readable without script.

no example exercises it

rule.links line 36 · specs/consumers/spec-studio.capability-map-page.sdp.md:36
Every node title links to that Spec's Studio page. A separate Show these Specs link goes to the index's Specs section with the epic selected. Keyed questions link to their entry on the Spec page; unkeyed questions link to the Spec page's section.intent. Unresolved endpoints are text with their diagnostics, never plausible Spec links.

no example exercises it

rule.filter line 37 · specs/consumers/spec-studio.capability-map-page.sdp.md:37
The index's Specs filter gains Epic, with Any, No epic and every epic by title and id. An epic selects its own Spec and every Spec whose full-corpus epicIds contains it. It intersects with the existing filters, resets with them, and never changes Pack membership or hides Pack cards.

no example exercises it

rule.withoutScript line 38 · specs/consumers/spec-studio.capability-map-page.sdp.md:38
Native links, disclosures, complete refinement text and all Spec rows work without script. Index filtering is an enhancement: before script applies a requested epic, the index says filtering needs script and shows all rows. A supplied id that is absent or not epic reports Unknown epic filter and leaves all rows visible.

no example exercises it

rule.emptyAndDamage line 39 · specs/consumers/spec-studio.capability-map-page.sdp.md:39
The page always has No epic reaches these Specs, including an explicit empty message. With no epics it explains that authors may organize Specs through refinement and still lists the whole corpus. Cycles and unresolved edges are visible diagnostics beside the complete text, without a new validation rule.

no example exercises it

0 unkeyed rules.

Design
route line 43 · specs/consumers/spec-studio.capability-map-page.sdp.md:43
capabilities.html; an epic's section id is its Spec id. The filtered-index route is index.html?epic=<percent-encoded Spec id>#specs; epic=none selects unreached Specs, absence selects Any. An unknown or repeated epic parameter reports the unknown-filter message without applying it.

no citation recorded

diagramInput line 44 · specs/consumers/spec-studio.capability-map-page.sdp.md:44
recipe 52's node, edge, epic and unreached rows supply the drawing and its text; layout derives no reach, floor or delivery fact. The shared drawing implementation owns folding, label metrics and SVG or Mermaid representation. A capability drawing must support same-altitude edges, skipped altitudes, multiple parents, nested epics, and cycles without pretending to be a strict three-level tree.
disclosureOrder line 45 · specs/consumers/spec-studio.capability-map-page.sdp.md:45
epic overview cards and sections follow recipe order. Each section opens with the epic's own rung, floor, binding evidence and questions, then the rollup labelled Distinct descendants, excluding this epic. Refinement text expands a depth-first walk with children in id order and renders later visits as references; it follows the recipe's root order and uses per-section visited ids. Examples and decisions fold through native disclosures without pruning their descendants.
rowEvidence line 46 · specs/consumers/spec-studio.capability-map-page.sdp.md:46
each row names kind and altitude, stated <rung>, floor <rung>, the implementation binding and the verifier binding as present or none, and open and blocking question counts with their text available. Facts that are absent stay absent; a folded branch's counts never become the parent's badges.
nestedEpics line 47 · specs/consumers/spec-studio.capability-map-page.sdp.md:47
a card for an epic that refines another epic says Inside <title>, using parentEpicIds, and a card whose descendants include an epic names it, so overlapping counts read as overlap.
responsive line 48 · specs/consumers/spec-studio.capability-map-page.sdp.md:48
overview cards reflow to one column on a narrow viewport; refinement text wraps ids and titles, caps visual indentation, and names the parent in words so deep trees remain readable. At desktop width diagram labels use the shared readable size and bounded branches. Below the responsive breakpoint the drawing follows the legibility rule's narrow fit; the complete refinement text is the readable form. Print opens the disclosures and retains the complete text.
Verification · reviewed
criteria
  • Read the same page on a corpus with one broad epic, several epics, and no epics, with script disabled and at a narrow viewport.
  • Follow a shared descendant from both parents and verify that the rollup counts it once and the index filter lists it once.
  • Select an epic on the index, combine it with kind and readiness filters, reset it, and open the filtered URL directly; invalid and repeated epic parameters never show a false empty result.

9. The Studio chooses diagram kinds from graph values

spec:consumers.spec-studio.diagram-kinds

The Studio chooses diagram kinds from graph values

spec:consumers.spec-studio.diagram-kindsUse Case / Behavior · featureready floor ready

Packs: pack:roadmaps-and-slices-v1, pack:self-hosting-v1

Design: 37 design entries · 1 pinned declaration · 1 decision

Findings: no errors, no warnings

specs/consumers/spec-studio.diagram-kinds.sdp.md

No open questions and no blocking questions; implementation binding present, verifier binding present, and expected-outcome oracle none.

Dependency chains across a Pack, capability refinement, the components a design touches, and differences between stated readiness and the floor need different pictures. A diagram kind earns its place through the question it answers and the graph values that answer it. Mermaid supplies a useful catalog of visual forms, not the Studio's layout runtime or an instruction to draw every form.

Intent
outcome
Choose useful drawings from graph values, keep their labels readable on first view, and offer source a reader can copy without changing the shipped Mermaid projection.
Behavior
rule.graphData line 22 · specs/consumers/spec-studio.diagram-kinds.sdp.md:22
A drawing reads the graph through the page's reader values and recipe answers. A visual form never supplies missing intent, order, cardinality, scores, dates or runtime evidence from prose, paths or imports.

no example exercises it

The catalog names each visual family, whether the graph holds its data, its subject, the question it answers, and a refusal or deferral's re-entry trigger. Renderer aliases share their family's row; diagnostic renderers are named apart.

Design
kindCatalog line 30 · specs/consumers/spec-studio.diagram-kinds.sdp.md:30
draw, equivalent, defer and refuse describe catalog choices only. They are not graph fields or delivery states. A deferred form has honest inputs but adds no needed reading beyond the selected views; a refused form lacks typed inputs.

no citation recorded

legibleLabels line 31 · specs/consumers/spec-studio.diagram-kinds.sdp.md:31
The figure keeps the Studio's navigation rail. Title-first labels and width-based cell wrapping reduce width; natural-size SVG with local horizontal scrolling preserves readable labels on desktop. Below the responsive breakpoint the same drawing fits the screen. The legibility child pins these measurements and behavior.
flowchart line 32 · specs/consumers/spec-studio.diagram-kinds.sdp.md:32
Draw for a Spec set, Pack, slice or roadmap from declared relations; dependency depth reveals chains and cycles the one-hop trace cannot show. Arrows retain their exact relation and direction, never execution order. The existing trace and members remain equivalent flowchart subjects.
mindmap line 33 · specs/consumers/spec-studio.diagram-kinds.sdp.md:33
Draw capability refinement from declared refines for an epic or capability map. The tree shows nesting absent from a flat list; repeated parents and cycles stay explicit rather than becoming an invented hierarchy.
treeView line 34 · specs/consumers/spec-studio.diagram-kinds.sdp.md:34
Equivalent to the capability tree for a strict refinement tree. Folder icons and file paths would invent meaning; use plain labels. Repeated parents use the capability view's cross-links or its flowchart source.
block line 35 · specs/consumers/spec-studio.diagram-kinds.sdp.md:35
Draw scoped architecture and the discrete maturity matrix. Components and anchored uses answer which seams a Spec set touches; stated and reached rungs answer where statements lag or overreach. Cell position is categorical, never a score.
architecture line 36 · specs/consumers/spec-studio.diagram-kinds.sdp.md:36
Equivalent to the scoped architecture drawing for a component or Spec set, from component, memberOf and uses plus planned-component declarations. Generic boxes keep optional context and layer; cloud, service, network and deployment icons need explicit typed declarations before they can mean anything.
usesTable line 37 · specs/consumers/spec-studio.diagram-kinds.sdp.md:37
Draw a component uses table, a design structure matrix, beside the architecture lens's drawing: one row per realized component as the user and one column per realized component as the used, in one order, a cell for each pair. A table stays legible at any number of uses, where routed edges between a dozen components run in parallel bundles. It is an HTML table read from anchored uses, needs no layout, bound or fold, and offers no Mermaid source because Mermaid has no matrix form.

Decisions

  • spec:decisions.studio-diagram-renderer

    The engine lays out every Studio diagram at build time with its own deterministic layered layout and writes it into the page as inline SVG followed by a text equivalent. The custom element that holds a diagram adds only pan, zoom and pinch, by changing the SVG's view box. One diagram draws at most the bound spec:consumers.spec-studio.diagrams names, and above it the diagram folds, by context and then by layer, as that Spec states.

specs/consumers/spec-studio.diagram-kinds.legibility.sdp.md

No open questions and no blocking questions; implementation binding present, verifier binding present, and expected-outcome oracle none.

Intent
outcome
Read a drawing's labels on first view while allowing a wide graph to scroll inside its figure.
Contract
rule.firstView line 19 · specs/consumers/spec-studio.diagram-kinds.legibility.sdp.md:19
At 720 CSS pixels of viewport width and wider, a diagram's SVG starts at its natural size inside its figure's scroll region and is never shrunk to fit. Overflow scrolls inside the figure, never the page. The build writes Scroll horizontally to read the whole drawing. above every drawing wider than the width budget. Below that viewport width the responsive contract's narrow drawing applies.

no example exercises it

rule.titleFirst line 20 · specs/consumers/spec-studio.diagram-kinds.legibility.sdp.md:20
A box starts with its title or recorded label at fourteen pixels, then a shortened id at twelve pixels, with full identity in its link title and text equivalent. Shortening changes no identity, target or element id; collisions extend the displayed suffix until it is unique within the figure. The box's remaining words, such as a component's member count, follow the id.

no example exercises it

0 unkeyed rules.

Design
widthBudget line 23 · specs/consumers/spec-studio.diagram-kinds.legibility.sdp.md:23
880 logical pixels for a band or grid, band labels included, which stay above their band; 264 per context cell when several contexts share a grid, the full band budget when only one context is shown, and 24 between boxes. A drawing wider than 880 scrolls inside its figure. Layout reads no browser or font measurement.

no citation recorded

labelMetrics line 24 · specs/consumers/spec-studio.diagram-kinds.legibility.sdp.md:24
Title lines hold at most 28 characters at fourteen pixels with an eight-pixel character advance; ids hold at most 30 characters at twelve pixels with an eight-pixel advance. Wrap at spaces or id punctuation, then by code point, with whole-pixel coordinates and height calculated from all lines.
minimumScale line 25 · specs/consumers/spec-studio.diagram-kinds.legibility.sdp.md:25
1 on first desktop view at viewport widths of at least 720 CSS pixels; below that width the responsive contract fits the same drawing to the screen. Zooming out on desktop remains an explicit reader choice.

no citation recorded

shortId line 26 · specs/consumers/spec-studio.diagram-kinds.legibility.sdp.md:26
Drop the namespace and the leading dotted segments every id in the figure shares, and mark the elision with a leading …, so a label may show …markdown-authoring; keep more segments on collisions. A displayed id never carries a namespace unless it is shown in full. Full ids remain in the link title, the text equivalent and the source.
viewport line 27 · specs/consumers/spec-studio.diagram-kinds.legibility.sdp.md:27
.diagram-scroll is a keyboard-focusable named region with overflow auto and max-width one hundred percent. At desktop widths its SVG has natural width and height with no max-width fit; below 720 CSS pixels the SVG fits the region. The caption and legend stay outside. The build emits the scroll instruction only when SVG width exceeds the fixed width budget; CSS leaves the region discoverable on narrower columns.

no citation recorded

elementIds line 28 · specs/consumers/spec-studio.diagram-kinds.legibility.sdp.md:28
Keep each kind's text and arrow ids; the viewport uses diagram.<subject>[.<view>].viewport and its visible instruction uses .scroll-help, inserting the view name exactly where the diagram's own ids do.

specs/consumers/spec-studio.diagram-kinds.edge-routing.sdp.md

No open questions and no blocking questions; implementation binding present, verifier binding present, and expected-outcome oracle none.

Intent
outcome
Follow an arrow without it crossing a box or covering a label, using the engine's own static layout.
Contract
rule.obstacles line 18 · specs/consumers/spec-studio.diagram-kinds.edge-routing.sdp.md:18
After box placement and label wrapping, reserve each box and band label rectangle as an obstacle with clearance. An edge may touch only its own source and destination ports; no other segment may intersect a reserved rectangle's interior.

no example exercises it

rule.routes line 19 · specs/consumers/spec-studio.diagram-kinds.edge-routing.sdp.md:19
Route edges deterministically in code-unit order by from, to, kind and claim with orthogonal whole-pixel paths around the reserved obstacles. Add no layout dependency and read no browser measurement. The build owns the search representation, weights and tie-break implementation.

no example exercises it

rule.ports line 20 · specs/consumers/spec-studio.diagram-kinds.edge-routing.sdp.md:20
Choose source and destination sides deterministically for forward, same-band and backward edges. Every incident edge has its own port. A cycle and a backward edge remain directed and route around intervening boxes.

no example exercises it

rule.labels line 21 · specs/consumers/spec-studio.diagram-kinds.edge-routing.sdp.md:21
Reserve an edge label's rectangle beside a free segment. If the exact relation and claim words do not fit, use a stable edge key and name its full wording in the adjacent legend and text equivalent. Every placed label rectangle is an obstacle for later labels and routes; no two labels overlap. An edge carries a label only where spec:consumers.spec-studio.diagrams asks for one; a drawing whose edges share one relation and one claim names them once in its legend.

no example exercises it

rule.noPath line 22 · specs/consumers/spec-studio.diagram-kinds.edge-routing.sdp.md:22
If any required route, distinct lane or label cannot be placed within the deterministic routing budget, omit that SVG and open its text equivalent with an explicit routing explanation. Never draw a straight line through a box as fallback.

no example exercises it

0 unkeyed rules.

Design
clearance line 25 · specs/consumers/spec-studio.diagram-kinds.edge-routing.sdp.md:25
12 logical pixels around boxes and text, with ports connected through their own clearance by a stub. Lane spacing is 8 pixels and gutter margin is 24 pixels; all coordinates and costs are integers.

no citation recorded

cost line 26 · specs/consumers/spec-studio.diagram-kinds.edge-routing.sdp.md:26
Crossings remain permitted at free points, never through nodes or labels. Two edges never share a collinear segment: they take distinct ports and lanes 8 pixels apart, and an edge that cannot get a lane is a routing failure under the no-path rule.
searchBound line 27 · specs/consumers/spec-studio.diagram-kinds.edge-routing.sdp.md:27
The build chooses a finite deterministic search budget and tests its routing-failure explanation; tuning the search changes no graph meaning. The shared box and edge bound applies first.
overflow line 28 · specs/consumers/spec-studio.diagram-kinds.edge-routing.sdp.md:28
Routing gutters may increase SVG width beyond the box layout budget to preserve distinct lanes; the desktop scroll instruction follows that final width. No label is shrunk to fit.
routeModel line 29 · specs/consumers/spec-studio.diagram-kinds.edge-routing.sdp.md:29
Each route retains from, to, kind, claim, optional aggregation count and relation reason, plus its integer point list; ports and routes are presentation values, never graph edges.
elementIds line 30 · specs/consumers/spec-studio.diagram-kinds.edge-routing.sdp.md:30
Preserve .edge data-from, data-to and data-kind, add data-claim when present and a stable data-edge-key for legend lookup; arrow marker ids remain scoped to subject and view.

specs/consumers/spec-studio.diagram-kinds.mermaid-source.sdp.md

No open questions and no blocking questions; implementation binding present, verifier binding present, and expected-outcome oracle none.

Mermaid source is a second serialization of the drawing's supplied values. It changes neither the static SVG renderer nor the separately shipped Mermaid root, so it requires no decision refining either ruling. A future Mermaid runtime, layout library or change to that root would need its own decision.

Intent
outcome
Copy a drawing into another document while keeping the Studio usable without script or a Mermaid runtime.
Behavior
rule.sourceOnly line 21 · specs/consumers/spec-studio.diagram-kinds.mermaid-source.sdp.md:21
Build escaped Mermaid text from the same selected and folded diagram values as the SVG. Source is an optional export, never a browser rendering path, a network request, a new command or a write to the shipped Mermaid root.

no example exercises it

rule.losslessMeaning line 22 · specs/consumers/spec-studio.diagram-kinds.mermaid-source.sdp.md:22
Each kind names its preferred syntax. Use a labelled flowchart fallback whenever that syntax cannot state the drawing's exact relations, claims or folds. State the chosen syntax and fallback reason beside the source. Preserve full ids in labels or comments and every aggregation count and folded member identity in comments; the text equivalent remains authoritative for the diagram's reading.

no example exercises it

rule.copy line 23 · specs/consumers/spec-studio.diagram-kinds.mermaid-source.sdp.md:23
A closed source disclosure contains a read-only text area with a visible label. Without script a reader selects and copies it. The page elements' copy control enhances this same text with its Copy button, Copied feedback and select-the-text fallback. The diagram element keeps only its viewport controls.

no example exercises it

rule.escaping line 24 · specs/consumers/spec-studio.diagram-kinds.mermaid-source.sdp.md:24
Treat every title, label, id and reason as data. Escape HTML at the page boundary and Mermaid syntax at the source boundary; never emit source directives, executable links, raw HTML or configuration supplied by corpus text.

no example exercises it

rule.omission line 25 · specs/consumers/spec-studio.diagram-kinds.mermaid-source.sdp.md:25
A drawing omitted for bounds or routing offers its text equivalent and a reason; it offers no partial Mermaid source that appears complete. Source follows the same explicit scope and folds as its figure.

no example exercises it

0 unkeyed rules.

Design
disclosure line 28 · specs/consumers/spec-studio.diagram-kinds.mermaid-source.sdp.md:28
Summary Mermaid source, a paragraph Copyable source; the Studio draws static SVG., a syntax label and optional fallback explanation, then a labelled read-only textarea and the script-added copy button.
sourceElement line 29 · specs/consumers/spec-studio.diagram-kinds.mermaid-source.sdp.md:29
The disclosure's copy button is the page elements' sdp-copy, given a for attribute that names the source text area so a long source is not repeated in an attribute; no new element is added, and sdp-diagram still adds only pan, zoom and pinch.

Decisions

  • spec:decisions.shipped-projections-frozen

    Re-specifying the shipped Design Review, census, Mermaid, or Gherkin projection is refused. These four projections are the ruled read surfaces over the one graph. A later decision Spec that supersedes this one replaces the ruling whole; a decision Spec that refines this one narrows it for one projection or one rendering and leaves the rest frozen. Either passes the ADR three-part test.

  • spec:decisions.studio-diagram-renderer

    The engine lays out every Studio diagram at build time with its own deterministic layered layout and writes it into the page as inline SVG followed by a text equivalent. The custom element that holds a diagram adds only pan, zoom and pinch, by changing the SVG's view box. One diagram draws at most the bound spec:consumers.spec-studio.diagrams names, and above it the diagram folds, by context and then by layer, as that Spec states.

18. A slice reads a Pack as one design, with the architecture it touches and what each member needs next

spec:consumers.design-slice

A slice reads a Pack as one design, with the architecture it touches and what each member needs next

spec:consumers.design-sliceUse Case / Behavior · featureready floor ready

Packs: pack:roadmaps-and-slices-v1, pack:self-hosting-v1

Design: 18 design entries · 15 pinned declarations · 2 decisions

Findings: no errors, no warnings

specs/consumers/design-slice.sdp.md

No open questions and no blocking questions; implementation binding present, verifier binding present, and expected-outcome oracle present.

Features that must be reviewed together are already grouped as a Pack, and the Pack page shows each member in turn. A design pass also needs the whole at once: how the members rest on each other, which components they touch, realized or planned, which decisions and open questions bound them, and what each member needs for its next rung. Rounds of design add detail a little at a time; the floor sets how little a rung needs, and how much is enough stays a judgment the authoring guidance supports and no check makes.

The first generation kept a slice as an authored file: a list of members and the one question they answer together, a saved view for design and review that delivered nothing itself (@libar-dev/architect, formal-spec/04-tag-registry.md, the hierarchy level slice). The original design saved AI context slices per Pack, per capability and per changed Spec as files (docs/lineage/v0-design/07-spec-studio-and-projections.md §5.5). The Protocol holds the first as a Pack, its members in reading order and its framing saying what they answer together, and it refused the second: a context bundle is composed on each invocation and never saved. A design slice is therefore a reading and not an artifact. It is a Pack read whole, narrowed to one perspective's members when a pass reads for one concern, or an ordered list of Specs, composed from the graph each time, and it adds no grouping, kind, stage or gate. A Spec's planning slice reads one Spec's neighborhood; widening it hop by hop would pick a reach no one authored, so a design slice starts from the set a person chose.

The reading answers what a card-by-card page leaves a reviewer to assemble. A design that builds on existing code says so through its own dependsOn or refines to the Spec that code satisfies, so the architecture a design ahead of its code will touch is read from those relations and the anchors of the Specs they name. The first adopter asked for the same separation: the design under review apart from the contracts and decisions it rests on, and the outside Spec whose rung holds a member shown at the boundary with what it holds (libar-platform/docs/feedback/sdp-feedback-02.md, items 11 and 12).

Intent
actor
A person or an agent running a design pass over features that must be reviewed together.
problem
The Pack page reads member by member, so a reviewer assembles the dependency order, the touched architecture and the open decisions by hand before judging the design as a whole.
outcome
Read a Pack as one design slice: its members and their relations, the components they touch, realized and planned, the decisions and open questions that bound them, and what each member needs for its next rung.
value
A design pass judges the whole before its parts, starting from the members others rest on, and sees how much design each member carries beside its rung without a score.
Behavior

Decisions

  • spec:decisions.anchor-binding-grain

    On a code anchor, satisfies is optional and plural; on a test anchor, verifies is plural and non-empty. The constant form accepts one ref(…) or a fresh array literal of them. Each resolving target confers its fact, and implemented stays a whole-Spec fact. An anchored edge references runs from a CodeNode to a Spec, from references?: readonly SpecId[] on a code anchor; it may target any Spec, decisions included, confers no delivery fact, moves no readiness floor, and the drift alarm ignores it. It says this code answers to that design without claiming to realize it: the unit follows the design without realizing any of its promises, or realizes part of a Spec whose remaining promises no unit yet realizes, so a change to the design asks the code to follow. A design that builds on existing code states that by a typed relation to the Spec the code satisfies, never by a reference from the code. A target named in both satisfies and references is an error. An identity-only code anchor, with no satisfies and no references, is lawful: it mints a CodeNode for structure and for byFile, and nothing else.

  • spec:decisions.architectural-annotation

    Architectural significance is annotated on the anchor of the unit that realizes it. A code anchor may carry role, the architectural pattern the unit plays; a component: anchor may additionally carry layer, one of edge, application, domain, adapter, or infrastructure, and context, its bounded context. The component: anchor is anchored architecture: it is the declared component, and there is no separate architecture file, because the anchor sits where the component is realized. It is not the original design's declared Component that could exist before code; an unrealized component lives in Specs and never as an invented CodeNode. A role is a free, corpus-owned vocabulary whose taxonomy the census renders with counts from the graph; service, decider, projection, read-model, codec, contract, barrel, and utility are the lineage set, not a closed list. layer is a closed set, and a value outside it is an envelope error; layer or context on a non-component anchor is an envelope error. All three attributes are optional, and omission is lawful.

33. A slice page shows a Pack's design as one whole

spec:consumers.spec-studio.slice-page

A slice page shows a Pack's design as one whole

spec:consumers.spec-studio.slice-pageUse Case / Behavior · storyready floor ready

Packs: pack:roadmaps-and-slices-v1, pack:self-hosting-v1

Design: 12 design entries · no pinned declarations · no decisions

Findings: no errors, no warnings

specs/consumers/spec-studio.slice-page.sdp.md

1 open question and no blocking questions; implementation binding present, verifier binding present, and expected-outcome oracle none.

The Pack page reads a Pack card by card, in the order its author wrote. A reviewer judging the design needs the other reading first: which members the rest stand on, what the design will touch in the code, and what decisions and questions bound it. The slice page gives that reading on a page of its own beside the Pack page, one link apart. It keeps the Pack page whole, because a Pack of a hundred members already makes a long page of cards, and the two readings answer different questions in different orders: the author's narrative there, the members others rest on first here.

Intent
outcome
Give the Studio a page per Pack that shows its design slice: the members' dependency drawing, the components they touch, the decisions and open questions in scope, and each member's next rung.

Open questions

  • non-blocking · question.exportCarriesSlice line 38 · specs/consumers/spec-studio.slice-page.sdp.md:38 · Does a Pack export also carry the Pack's slice page?Decider: delegatedProvisional: no; the export keeps the Pack page and its members, and the slice page stays one link away in the page set
Behavior
rule.slicePerPack line 44 · specs/consumers/spec-studio.slice-page.sdp.md:44
The page set holds one slice page per Pack, slices/<name>.html, its name formed from the Pack's id as the Pack page's name is; it renders the build's design slice answer for that Pack in full and states no value the answer does not hold, apart from counts the build takes of it.

no example exercises it

rule.header line 45 · specs/consumers/spec-studio.slice-page.sdp.md:45
The page opens with the heading Design slice and the Pack's title, the Pack's id as text with a copy action, and a link back to the Pack page, then the summary and a reading note.

no example exercises it

rule.summary line 46 · specs/consumers/spec-studio.slice-page.sdp.md:46
The summary states each slice total in one sentence that opens with its count: the members and the examples counted in their parents; the relations among members, the deepest depth and any cycle; the members held below their stated next rung and those waiting only for their author; the outside Specs the slice rests on, how many of them hold a member, and the outside Specs that rest on it; the components touched, through the members' code, through what the slice rests on, and named by member designs, with the outside components shown beside them; the member component designs, how many are realized and how many of those match; the decisions in scope and how many state below ready; and the open and blocking questions.

no example exercises it

rule.readingNote line 47 · specs/consumers/spec-studio.slice-page.sdp.md:47
The reading note says in words that members read with the ones others rest on first, that the design columns count what each member carries beside its rung and never judge whether it is enough, and that the page records no review and approves nothing.

no example exercises it

rule.dependencyDrawing line 48 · specs/consumers/spec-studio.slice-page.sdp.md:48
Under How the members rest on each other comes the slice's dependency drawing, spec:consumers.spec-studio.diagram-kinds.dependency given the slice's order: it consumes the answer's members, depths, rests-on links, structure edges, cycles and boundary rows and recomputes no scope, depth or order. Each member that is not a folded example is a box with its title, id, stated rung and floor, and its count of folded example members; every supplied relation keeps its type and direction, and a relation that orders nothing reads apart from one that orders. The drawing kind owns layout, bounded folding and the complete text equivalent, which lists every folded example with its refines; a fold changes no value of the answer.

no example exercises it

rule.memberTable line 49 · specs/consumers/spec-studio.slice-page.sdp.md:49
Under What each member needs next comes one row per member that is not a folded example, by depth and then in the scope's order: the member's title linked to its card on the Pack page with its id, its depth, its stated rung beside the floor reached, its stated next rung with nothing blocks or each unmet clause and the Specs it names with their stated rungs, then the design it carries, its rules with how many are keyed, its design entries, pinned declarations, open questions with how many block, decisions, and verifying examples with how many are bound, each count on its own line, and its implementation and reference bindings as counts; the table has no total row, and no count is combined with another.

rule.exampleRows line 50 · specs/consumers/spec-studio.slice-page.sdp.md:50

Folding lends the parent no rung, hold or binding, and the folded count stays apart from the count of examples that verify the parent.

34. A roadmap states advisory priority in the graph

spec:decisions.roadmap-priority

A roadmap states advisory priority in the graph

spec:decisions.roadmap-priorityDecision Record · featureready floor ready

Packs: pack:roadmaps-and-slices-v1, pack:self-hosting-v1

Design: no design entries · no pinned declarations · no decisions

Findings: no errors, no warnings

specs/decisions/roadmap-priority.sdp.md

No open questions and no blocking questions; implementation binding none, verifier binding none, and expected-outcome oracle none.

Dependency order already has a graph home: dependsOn, which the statement queue reads to order the statements a person can make. Preference has none: which body of work the owner wants next when nothing forces one before another. It lives in prose, in each pull request's forward section and in the plan files, and the graph reads neither. The roadmap views waited for a named reader; the owner, choosing what the next pull requests take up, is that reader. A Pack already keeps its members in authored order and states no truth of its own, so a Pack whose manifest says its order is a priority holds the preference with one optional field and no new relation.

Intent
outcome
Decide whether and how the graph may hold an advisory priority over upcoming work, a roadmap, without dates, without a new relation, and without gating or sequencing any work.
Decision
context
The planning truths decision gives each planning truth a ruled graph home and keeps recorded work order out of the graph, so dependency rides dependsOn and everything else about order stays in plan files and pull request descriptions. The owner now reads and edits that order and asks for it in the graph: what to design next and a prioritized list of what to build, tied to the pull requests that carry it out. A Pack keeps its members in authored order and states no system truth; the Pack manifest's envelope is closed to id, specs and modelRefs.
decision
A roadmap is a Pack whose manifest states order: priority; its members' authored order is the corpus's advisory priority, first entry first. order is an optional manifest field whose one lawful value is priority, and a Pack without it keeps the reading order every Pack has. Priority is preference among bodies of work and nothing more: it carries no date, no dependency, no status and no gate, and no check, recipe or page treats a place on a roadmap as permission, obligation or sequence. Everything a roadmap shows about an entry, what it still needs and what holds it, is read from the graph each time. A corpus may keep several roadmaps, and a Spec may be listed on any number of them.
rationale
  • Hard to reverse: the manifest envelope gains a field that both manifest carriers, the graph's Pack node and the reader carry, and corpora author roadmaps against it. Surprising without context: the planning truths decision kept recorded work order out of the graph, so a reader needs to know why one order is now graph data and why it still sequences nothing. A real trade-off: a priority held in the graph is checked where membership is checked, so every entry resolves; it shows in the design diff, as an added, removed or reordered member and as a Pack that becomes or stops being a roadmap; and it reaches the Studio, the vault and a pull request's forward section with no extra input. It costs one optional field and the risk that an order reads as a schedule, which this decision bounds by giving the order no consequence.
  • A Pack is the right home because a roadmap says nothing about the system. It is an authored grouping, as a Pack is, whose members already carry an authored order; the field states what that order means and leaves the rest of the Pack law unchanged.
alternatives
  • A Pack read as a roadmap by a naming convention, such as a reserved id: the Protocol reads no meaning from an id anywhere else, a reserved name would collide with a corpus's own Packs, and nothing in the manifest would tell its reader that the order means priority.
  • Any Pack's order read as a priority, the roadmap named to each recipe and page as a parameter: the Studio takes no corpus configuration, so it could not tell a roadmap from a Pack in reading order, and a reading order would show as a priority nobody stated.
  • Priority outside the graph, as corpus data a recipe reads, like a perspective's order: an entry that no longer resolves is caught only by a rules file the corpus writes, the design diff, the Studio, the vault and the preview workflow would each need a new input to see it, and planning would gain a second store beside the graph. A perspective suits a reader's own concern; a roadmap is one authored choice for the whole corpus.
  • A new relation such as precedes, or a rank on each Spec: the planning truths decision refused precedes for its engine surface across the model, the carriers, extraction, validators and the agent surface, and a rank on the truth primitive is a status that goes stale with every edit and invites scoring.
  • A boolean field such as roadmap: true: it names the noun but not what differs, which is the meaning of the order; order: priority says that directly.
  • Prose, as today: the graph cannot read it, and each forward section is rewritten by hand and drifts from the Specs it names.
consequences
  • The planning truths decision's refusal of recorded work order narrows for this one case: a roadmap's priority is graph structure, carried as its Pack's member order, and never workflow authority. Plan numbering, staleness and every other recorded work order stay out of the graph.
  • The Pack manifest admits order, in the Markdown and the TypeScript manifest alike; the Pack node carries order when the manifest states it, after modelRefs in the serialized node; any other value refuses at extraction as a malformed envelope field does; and the Pack model names the priority order. These touch the Pack carrier, the Pack model and the Pack node's member-order law, each enriched in place when the field is built.
  • No check reads a roadmap's content. An entry already built, an order that disagrees with dependency, an empty roadmap and several roadmaps are never findings, because a place carries no authority and staleness is never a finding.
  • Where priority and dependency disagree, a roadmap view shows what an entry rests on and never reorders it; readiness statements keep the statement queue's dependency order, in a roadmap's list of what waits on a person as everywhere else.
  • The design diff reports a change in what a Pack's order means apart from a change in its members' order, so a Pack that becomes or stops being a roadmap shows in a comparison even when its members stay. A base graph whose schema predates the field carries no order and reads as reading order, as an absent field does in every schema version; a value the head's engine does not know lies outside the common schema and is reported as a diagnostic, never compared. This touches the design diff and its Studio page when the field is built.
  • A place on a roadmap confers what membership of any Pack confers, which is nothing: no readiness, no delivery fact and no gate.
  • The roadmap reading, its page and its forward-section memo read a roadmap this way, under spec:consumers.roadmap.

35. A roadmap orders the next bodies of work, and the graph says what each still needs

spec:consumers.roadmap

A roadmap orders the next bodies of work, and the graph says what each still needs

spec:consumers.roadmapUse Case / Behavior · featureready floor ready

Packs: pack:roadmaps-and-slices-v1, pack:self-hosting-v1

Design: 13 design entries · 10 pinned declarations · 1 decision

Findings: no errors, no warnings

specs/consumers/roadmap.sdp.md

No open questions and no blocking questions; implementation binding present, verifier binding present, and expected-outcome oracle present.

The Protocol's planning reads the graph: the build backlog lists ready work no code realizes, the design backlog lists defined work, and the statement queue orders what a person can state. None of them says which capability comes first. A roadmap is that one authored choice, the order of the next few bodies of work. Everything else about an entry, whether it still needs design, waits only for a person's statement, is ready to build, or is built, is read from the graph each time, so a roadmap never goes stale in what it says about state. It goes stale only in its order, which its owner edits.

An entry stands for its whole refinement subtree: an epic for its features and stories, a feature for its stories. The reading counts the subtree's work by what each part needs, so a large entry shows how much of it is designed and built, and the parts that could be built now.

Intent
actor
The owner choosing what the next pull requests take up, and an agent opening the next body of work.
problem
Priority lives in prose, in each pull request's forward section and in the plan files, which the graph cannot read and which go stale as work lands.
outcome
Read a roadmap as an ordered list of upcoming capabilities, each placed by the graph in what it needs next, to design, to state, to build or built, with the design it lacks and the work it rests on.
Behavior

rule.waiting line 45 · specs/consumers/roadmap.sdp.md:45
Apart from the entries, the reading lists what waits on the person the caller names, the owner by default: each open question whose decider names that person, on a Spec of any entry's scope or on a decision a scope names by decidedBy; and each such Spec or decision whose floor reaches a rung above the rung it states, a statement only a person makes, which for a decision is its ratification. Each row carries the places of the entries it touches. Questions follow their first place; statements keep their relative order in the statement queue across the whole roadmap, so a Spec others rest on comes first whatever its place, and their places never reorder them.

Design view

Requirement drawing

Decisions

  • A roadmap states advisory priority in the graph

    A roadmap is a Pack whose manifest states order: priority; its members' authored order is the corpus's advisory priority, first entry first. order is an optional manifest field whose one lawful value is priority, and a Pack without it keeps the reading order every Pack has. Priority is preference among bodies of work and nothing more: it carries no date, no dependency, no status and no gate, and no check, recipe or page treats a place on a roadmap as permission, obligation or sequence. Everything a roadmap shows about an entry, what it still needs and what holds it, is read from the graph each time. A corpus may keep several roadmaps, and a Spec may be listed on any number of them.

The roadmap page shows the upcoming work in priority order, split by what it needs

specs/consumers/spec-studio.roadmap-page.sdp.md

No open questions and no blocking questions; implementation binding present, verifier binding present, and expected-outcome oracle none.

The owner reads a roadmap to choose what the next pull requests take up, and a reviewer reads it to see where an arc stands. The page shows each roadmap at a glance as a board, its entries in the column of what each needs next, and then each entry with what holds it. It ends with the forward section a pull request description carries, ready to copy. The page orders by the owner's places and links; it states nothing.

Intent
actor
The owner choosing the next work, and a reviewer with only a link.
problem
No page shows what comes next in priority order, so the owner reads it from the last pull request description, and a reviewer cannot tell which upcoming work needs design, a statement or a build.
outcome
Give the Studio a page that shows each roadmap in its priority order, with what to design, what to state, what to build and what is built, and for each entry what it lacks.
Behavior

46. A roadmap renders as the forward section of a pull request description

spec:consumers.roadmap.memo

A roadmap renders as the forward section of a pull request description

spec:consumers.roadmap.memoUse Case / Behavior · storyready floor ready

Packs: pack:roadmaps-and-slices-v1, pack:self-hosting-v1

Design: 11 design entries · no pinned declarations · no decisions

Findings: no errors, no warnings

specs/consumers/roadmap.memo.sdp.md

No open questions and no blocking questions; implementation binding present, verifier binding present, and expected-outcome oracle none.

A pull request description ends with a forward section: the next work in priority order, what waits on the owner, and what is deferred until its trigger. Written by hand, it drifts from the Specs it names and is rewritten each time. The roadmap memo renders it from the roadmap reading at the head of the branch, so the forward section a description carries is the roadmap the graph holds. The memo states what the graph holds and nothing more: it copies each entry's purpose from its own intent and derives its dependency reach, and the owner's reason for an entry's place, the re-entry condition of the next pull request and the durable refused list stay the description author's words around it.

Intent
actor
The author of a pull request description, and the owner reading it.
problem
A description's forward section is written by hand from plan files and recipe answers, so it drifts from the roadmap and the Specs it names.
outcome
Render a roadmap's entries, what waits on the owner and the deferred questions as Markdown a pull request description carries as its forward section, so the plan a description proposes is the roadmap the graph holds.
Behavior

47. Plan and review files stop carrying the delivery record once the roadmap and the pull request do

spec:decisions.roadmap-over-plans

Plan and review files stop carrying the delivery record once the roadmap and the pull request do

spec:decisions.roadmap-over-plansDecision Record · featureready floor ready

Packs: pack:roadmaps-and-slices-v1, pack:self-hosting-v1

Design: no design entries · no pinned declarations · no decisions

Findings: no errors, no warnings

specs/decisions/roadmap-over-plans.sdp.md

No open questions and no blocking questions; implementation binding none, verifier binding none, and expected-outcome oracle none.

Each arc's intent already lives in its capture Specs and its Pack, its rulings in their carrying Specs, its open items in keyed questions, and its story in its pull request description. A plan file still carries the status line the handbook copies and agents read first, the arc's lanes and waves, copies of its ruling tables, and its acceptance as measured. Beside it, committed review reports and their assets carry a review's findings, what became of each, and the screenshots and prototypes the review cites, while a change proposal already gives a finding against a Spec its reviewable shape. Once a roadmap holds priority in the graph and the pull request holds the arc's story and its reviews, the forward role and the record each have one home; what remains of a plan or a review file is history, or a second copy of what the graph, git and the pull request description already hold. Retiring the files removes competing records, never durable evidence.

Intent
outcome
Decide whether the Protocol retires its numbered plan files and its committed review files, reading its next work from the roadmap and keeping each arc's record in git and its pull request, and what replaces the gate that requires a current plan.
Decision
context
Plan files grew as the Protocol's working record: every arc adds one, the handbook keeps a status line for each, and the self-hosting gate requires the highest-numbered plan to carry a status header the handbook names. Review reports grew beside them under reviews/, with their prompts and assets. Since the graph-first planning arc, a plan is a thin pointer to its Pack and capture Specs, and the pull request description standard already asks each description for the arc's story, its rulings as tables, its acceptance as measured and a forward section. The owner asked whether plans can be replaced by Specs: no prose in the plan, but designed, grouped and prioritized roadmaps and sets of features or epics. The owner then retired both folders as carriers of the delivery record, leaving their removal or archival to a separate cleanup change.
decision
The Protocol reads its forward planning from its roadmap and keeps its delivery record in git and its pull requests; it adds no plan file and no review file, and plans/ and reviews/ stand as frozen history until a later arc removes or archives them. An agent opening the next work runs the roadmap recipe over the roadmap Pack the handbook names and follows each entry to its Packs and carrying Specs. Before an arc's first push its record is its branch, git being the event log: the arc's first commit message states the owner's working rules for the arc and the arc's Pack, each later message says what its unit did, and outstanding work is read from the arc's Pack, the backlogs and the open-question register; no record file is kept under reviews/ or anywhere else. The arc pushes and opens its draft pull request at its first coherent commit, normally the scaffold, so the window in which only local git holds the record stays short and a session restarted on another machine sees the work. The draft pull request description then holds the arc's narrative: its story, lanes, rulings with who made them, review findings as change proposals and their memos, acceptance as measured, deferrals and refusals. A review's findings against Specs travel as a change proposal whose base is the branch-head commit the reviewer read, never a preview's merge commit, checked against that base and posted to the pull request as its memo; a finding against code or another file is a review comment on its line; a finding left open becomes an open question with its decider, provisional reading and links. Evidence no test or recipe carries is committed on the arc's branch with the commands that made it, linked from the description at that commit, and removed before the merge, which keeps the commit reachable. Briefs and prompts stay in the session. The handbook names the roadmap Pack and the roadmap recipe where it named the current plan, and the self-hosting gate checks that instead of a current plan.
rationale
  • Hard to reverse: the handbook, the skills, the description standard and a gate point every session at the newest plan and at committed review files, and every session's first read changes. Surprising without context: a reader finds two folders that stopped. A real trade-off: one forward-planning carrier in the graph and one record per arc in git and its pull request, with nothing to keep in step, against review findings and pre-push state living in commit messages and pull request threads rather than in files a person can search in the tree.
alternatives
  • Keep plan files for forward planning beside the roadmap: priority would live in two places, and the plan's copy would drift.
  • Keep a thin plan file per arc for its execution record alone, with no status gate: the pull request description already carries the same record by the description standard, so the file would be a second copy that the next session must reconcile.
  • Record an arc's execution in the graph, as an arc Spec or Pack fields: who ruled what and when is history that git and the description keep, and that a review happened is never a graph fact.
  • A gate check that refuses a numbered plan past the last frozen one: the cleanup arc removes the folder, so the check would guard a short window, and refusing a kind of file polices the workflow, not conformance; the handbook saying the plans are frozen history is enough.
  • Keep an arc's record in a file under reviews/ until its first push, then only its link: the file repeats what the commits already say, outlives the arc as a stub, and keeps reviews/ growing after its retirement.
  • Keep review reports as committed files beside the change proposal: the proposal is the reviewable shape, an applied edit is git history and an open finding is an open question, so a report file repeats all three and goes stale with the next edit.
  • Keep evidence no test or recipe carries in a committed evidence folder on the main line: the folder becomes a new store that grows with every arc, while a link pinned to the arc's commit already lasts after the merge.
  • Link only the latest preview or an expiring CI artifact as evidence: a later run replaces what a historical description cites.
consequences
  • The handbook drops its stack of plan statuses for a short pointer to the roadmap and its recipe. The self-hosting gate's current-record check refuses a handbook that does not name the roadmap Pack and recipe, and a roadmap Pack manifest that is missing or does not state priority order; its frozen historical checks, its green-gate legs and its ban on plan status in the registry and the glossary stay until the cleanup arc removes the folders they read. It adds no check of plan numbers, roadmap content, work order, freshness or review disposition.
  • The graph-first planning Spec's plan-file rule narrows to a plan document a corpus chooses to keep, which points to its Packs and carrying Specs and confers nothing; an adopter keeps whatever planning documents it wants, and a roadmap is open to it as to the Protocol.
  • The description standard renders its forward section with the roadmap memo; the pull request that completes an entry's selected work removes it from the roadmap in the same change, and entries join or move only on the owner's word.
  • The owner's instruction that opens an arc authorizes commits on its branch, as a plan's commit strategy did, and its push; this record convention creates no authority of its own. The arc's first commit message records the owner's working rules and the draft description repeats them. A session that must stop with no clean boundary commits its work in progress on the arc's branch with a message saying what is incomplete, rather than accounting for it in a file; a session resuming without its predecessor reads the branch, its commits, the draft pull request and the graph, and never claims git kept what was never committed.
  • The proposal schema still scopes Specs only: a finding that changes no Spec takes no invented Spec scope, and a review that proposes no Spec edit needs no empty proposal. An accepted change is an ordinary carrier edit, and whether a change was accepted stays in the pull request's discussion and git, never in the proposal or the graph.
  • Tests and recipes carry repeatable evidence. A preview is the current human view of a branch, never an immutable acceptance record, so the description names the commit it measured and the commands that re-derive each number.
  • The plan and review files stay as they are until a dedicated cleanup arc removes or archives them and updates the historical checks and links that read them; until then nothing is added to either, and a file in either changes only to correct the record it keeps. This decision sets no record convention for an adopter.

specs/protocol/roadmap-replaces-plans.sdp.md

No open questions and no blocking questions; implementation binding present, verifier binding present, and expected-outcome oracle none.

Each arc's intent already lives in its capture Specs and Pack, its rulings in their carrying Specs, and its story in its pull request description. What a plan file still carries is the status line agents read first, the lanes and waves of the arc, and copies of ruling tables; what a committed review file carries, a change proposal, its memo and git already hold. Once a roadmap holds priority, the Protocol reads its next work from the graph, keeps each arc's record in git and its pull request, with review findings and evidence beside the story, and lets the plan and review files stand as the record of how earlier arcs were run. The Protocol keeps one living roadmap: its owner selects what it lists, and the pull requests that complete that work remove it.

The handbook points every session at the newest plan file and keeps a status line for each, and a gate requires both, so forward planning lives in prose beside the graph that already holds the arc's intent, and committed review files repeat what change proposals, git and the pull request already carry.
outcome
Let an agent opening the Protocol's next work read it from the roadmap recipe, review and recover an arc from git and its pull request, and keep the plan and review files as frozen history no gate requires to grow.
